paragraphs: Regarding what we say, 'and You are destined to take it from me,' etc. — the intention is as our teacher, may his memory be blessed, wrote in the book Peri Etz Chayim, page 9: that the attribute of Malkhut takes the souls of Israel at night, during sleep, and returns them in the morning, in the secret of 'new every morning' (Job 3:23), and this matter is a great benefit for the soul, as is known. Therefore, when a person awakens, he gives thanks and praise for this benefit which he will attain on the coming night, and he thanks for the future, saying 'You are destined to take it from me at night' — meaning that the soul will ascend in the secret of mayin nukvin (feminine waters) to Malkhut, and to return it to me in the morning in the secret of 'new every morning,' as he further wrote in Sefer HaKavanot, in the discourses on the night, page 77 column 4, regarding this secret of the verse 'new every morning' — that the souls of those below ascend every night to the Heichal and become enclothed within Malkhut, and afterward in the morning they emerge from there renewed, see there. And so it is likewise explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be blessed, in Sha'ar Ma'amarei Rashbi, in the explanation of Idra Zuta, page 51, where he wrote as follows: 'Every single night the souls of those below ascend in the secret of "Into Your hand I entrust my spirit" (Psalms 31:6) at the time of lying down, and the supernal Malkhut becomes pregnant with them in the secret of "new every morning, great is Your faithfulness," and the benefit and purpose of this is to renew those souls and give them strength and illuminate them; and this renewal is what renews and repairs the person's faculties (mochin), which is the aspect of the soul that dwells in the brain, as is known' — until here his words. Behold, this matter has been explained to you well. And know that although our teacher, may his memory be blessed, wrote in Chayei Olam HaBa there that the souls of those below cannot ascend in the secret of mayin nukvin at night as mentioned above except once a person is thirteen years and one day old, but below that age no soul at all is able to ascend in the secret of mayin nukvin — and if so, according to this one may ask: how do minors under thirteen say this thanksgiving of the morning blessings mentioned above, which does not apply to them? Behold, on this one may say that since minors are included within adults, they are able to recite this blessing; and similar to this is found in the words of our Sages, that a person may recite the morning blessings even though he is not obligated in them, for they were instituted according to the general custom of the world (minhago shel olam); and although in this blessing one gives thanks about himself and does not speak in the third person — behold there are other blessings in which one blesses about oneself even though the situation described does not apply to him, such as the blessing of HaMaavir (who removes sleep) even though he did not sleep at all, and likewise the blessing 'she'asah li kol tzorki' recited by a mourner — the same applies regarding the blessing of minors. Let us return to the first matter, to further explain why we say this thanksgiving in future tense and not in past tense: it would be fitting for a person to give thanks for the past, for what the Holy One, blessed be He, did in kindness with him on this very night of the day in which he now stands, when rising from his sleep, that He returned his soul to him and renewed it in his brain. Behold, in truth, this thanksgiving was instituted in future tense in order to include within it another intention, namely: that in the future to come, likewise, Malkhut will take the souls of the righteous in the secret of mayin nukvin, and they will return to be renewed in a most exalted perfection, the like of which there is none; and therefore these words 'le'atid lavo' (in the future to come) were added to this thanksgiving, for it would have sufficed to say 'to take it from me and to return it to me,' but he added the words 'le'atid lavo' in order to include within it this second intention mentioned, that we intend in this thanksgiving of ours to thank the Blessed Name also for the exalted good which He will do for us in the future to come, which is similar to this good which He does with us at this time every night and day. And see in the book Peri Etz Chayim, which wrote in explanation of this blessing, and this is his language: 'and also in the future it will be so,' see there; and likewise in the siddur of our teacher HaRashash, may his memory be blessed, it is written thus: 'destined to take it from me for mayin nukvin, and to return it to me every morning, and also in the future to come' — until here, see there.

clarification.explanation:
Regarding what is said in the blessing 'Elohai Neshamah,' 'You are destined to take it from me' — the intention (based on Peri Etz Chayim): the attribute of Malkhut takes the souls of Israel at night during sleep and returns them in the morning, in the secret of 'new every morning,' and this is a great benefit for the soul — for it ascends in the secret of mayin nukvin (feminine waters) to Malkhut, is renewed there, and emerges in the morning renewed and illuminated (so too in Sha'ar Ma'amarei Rashbi, Idra Zuta). Therefore when a person awakens he gives thanks for this benefit — and in future tense, for what he will merit on the coming night.
And although the Ari wrote that souls cannot ascend in the secret of mayin nukvin except from the age of thirteen years and one day — one might ask, how then do minors recite this thanksgiving? Rather, minors, since they are included within adults, may recite it; and further, a person may recite the morning blessings even though he was not obligated in them, for they were instituted 'according to the custom of the world' (like 'HaMaavir sheinah,' recited even by one who did not sleep, and 'she'asah li kol tzorki' recited by a mourner).
And the reason it is said in future tense and not past tense (although it would be fitting to give thanks for the kindness of the previous night) — is to include an additional intention: that in the future to come, Malkhut will take the souls of the righteous in the secret of mayin nukvin and they will return to be renewed in supreme perfection beyond compare; therefore 'le'atid lavo' (in the future to come) was added, to thank God also for the exalted good He will do for us in the future, similar to that done every night (so too in the siddur of the Rashash).
takeaways: 'You are destined to take it' — Malkhut takes the soul at night (mayin nukvin) and returns it renewed in the morning ('new every morning'), and this is a great benefit.

Minors recite this even though according to the secret this ascent applies only from age 13 — because they are included within adults, and because the morning blessings were instituted according to the custom of the world.
It is said in future tense — to include also a thanksgiving for the exalted good that will be given to the righteous in the future to come.

paragraphs: This blessing of 'Elohai' etc. should be juxtaposed to the blessing of 'Asher Yatzar,' for this blessing must be adjacent to its companion, and there is a secret in this matter mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot; and one must pause slightly between the word 'Elohai' and the word 'Neshamah,' so that it not be understood that the soul is his god, God forbid. And one should not say 'tehorah hi' (it is pure) but rather say 'tehorah, atah bera'atah' (pure — You created it), and so forth, as mentioned in the Acharonim. And as for the ending 'to dead corpses' (pegarim meitim) — thus are called the bodies that are idle from their work and cease from their movement, for 'peger' is a term of cessation, as in 'asher pigru me'avor' (1 Samuel 30:10), and likewise in the language of our Sages, 'pigrei rabbanan.' And as for saying 'meitim' (dead) — because sleep is one-sixtieth of death, and it is a sign for the resurrection of the dead in the future, as mentioned in the siddur of Rav Ya'avetz, may his memory be blessed. And know that this blessing has forty-seven words, corresponding to the numerical value of Havayah and Ehyeh, as our teacher HaRashash, may his memory be blessed, wrote; therefore one should not say the two words 'she'atah hu kodem Ribon kol hama'asim' as written in the siddurim, but rather say 've'Elohei avotai Ribon kol hama'asim.'

clarification.explanation: The blessing 'Elohai Neshamah' should be juxtaposed to the blessing 'Asher Yatzar' (there is a secret in this). One should pause slightly between 'Elohai' and 'Neshamah' (so that it not be understood, God forbid, that the soul is his god). One does not say 'tehorah hi' (it is pure), but rather 'tehorah, atah bera'atah' (pure — You created it). 'Pegarim meitim' (dead corpses) — the body idle from labor during sleep (from the language of 'cessation'). The comparison of sleep to death (one-sixtieth of death) is a sign for the future resurrection of the dead. The blessing contains forty-seven words (corresponding to the numerical value of Havayah and Ehyeh); and one says 've'Elohei avotai Ribon kol hama'asim' (not 'she'atah hu... kodem Ribon').
takeaways: The blessing 'Elohai Neshamah': pause between 'Elohai' and 'Neshamah'; say 'tehorah, atah bera'atah' (not 'tehorah hi'), and 've'Elohei avotai Ribon kol hama'asim.'

paragraphs: One should take care to have intention in the blessing when mentioning the Name Havayah, which is pronounced as the Name Adonai, that he picture in his mind the letters of the Name Havayah, and within the final letter Hei picture the Name Adonai; and he should also picture the combined Name of Havayah-Adonai. And how good and pleasant it is to be careful about this every time one mentions the Name, whether in verses or in prayer. And one must also be careful, when mentioning the Name Havayah, to picture in his mind the letters of the Name with their vowel points, and in the siddurim and Chumashim it is customary to vocalize it with the vocalization of 'le'olam,' and anyone who prays and studies verses from a book — this will be easy for him without difficulty. And one should be careful not to begin saying 'Baruch' until he has thought in his heart and knows for what he is blessing, as mentioned by the Acharonim, may their memory be blessed.

clarification.explanation: When mentioning the Name Havayah (which is read as 'Adonai'), one should picture in thought the letters of the Name Havayah, and within the final Hei picture the Name Adonai (the combination of the two Names) — at every mention, in verses and in prayer. One should also picture the vocalization (as it is customarily vocalized as 'le'olam' in the siddurim) — therefore one who studies from a book does this easily. One should not begin to say 'Baruch' before he knows in his thought for what he is blessing.
takeaways: When mentioning God's Name, one should picture in thought the letters of the Name (Havayah combined with Adonai) and its vocalization.
One should not begin to bless before knowing well for what one is blessing.

paragraphs: The blessing 'Who gives the rooster (sechvi) understanding' — according to its plain meaning, 'sechvi' is the rooster, which knows this understanding to distinguish between day and night, meaning between midday and midnight, for if not so, what is its advantage over other living creatures, as mentioned in Shalmei Tzibbur. But according to the words of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be blessed, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, 'sechvi' is the secret of Gevurah, which is called sechvi, and at midnight the illumination of Binah is drawn upon Gevurah, and then it is sweetened; and it is known that 'leil' (evening/night) is called before midnight, and 'lailah' (night) after midnight; therefore this blessing is recited from after midnight onward, see there. And in the kavanot of our teacher HaRashash, may his memory be blessed, he concluded that one must distinguish between the attribute of day, which is the secret of the male (dechura), called the attribute of day, for now begins the time of its repair, which is from midnight until midday; and the attribute of night, which is the female (nukva), called the attribute of night, whose repair is already completed, which is from midday until midnight, see there. And it is clear that even a deaf person who does not hear at all recites this blessing; see Minchat Aharon, Klal 5, letter 12.

clarification.explanation: The blessing 'HaNotein LaSechvi Binah' — according to the plain meaning, 'sechvi' is the rooster that distinguishes between day and night (otherwise what advantage would it have over other animals?). According to the Ari, 'sechvi' is the secret of the attribute of Gevurah, and from it the illumination of Binah is drawn at midnight and sweetens it — therefore this blessing is recited only after midnight. And our teacher the Rashash added a further reason for the distinction between before midnight and after: one must distinguish between the 'attribute of day,' which is the secret of the male, whose time of repair begins specifically from midnight until midday, and the 'attribute of night,' which is the secret of the female, whose repair is already completed from midday until midnight — and since the repair of the day only begins at midnight, this is the proper time to bless on the distinction between the two. Even a deaf person who does not hear at all recites this blessing.
takeaways: The blessing 'HaNotein LaSechvi Binah' is recited only after midnight (based on the secret, the sweetening of Gevurah by the illumination of Binah).

According to the Rashash: from midnight the repair of the 'attribute of day' (the male) begins, while the 'attribute of night' (the female) had already completed its repair beforehand — and this is why this is the proper time for the blessing.
A deaf person also recites this blessing.

paragraphs: The blessing 'Pokei'ach Ivrim' (Who gives sight to the blind) is a thanksgiving for His kindness, blessed be He, that a person's eyes were closed and shut in sleep, and when he awakens his eyes are opened. And behold, regarding a blind person there is a dispute among the poskim whether he should recite this blessing or not, and the Gaon Chida in Shiyurei Berachah agreed that we hold he should bless, and so wrote the proofreading Rabbi in Shalmei Tzibbur, see there. And in truth, although we hold that in a case of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient (safek berachot lehakel), here we hold that he should bless, because according to the opinion of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be blessed, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, all these blessings were instituted according to the custom of the world, and even though a person was not obligated in them he must bless — if so, the same applies to a blind person, that he must bless; and against the reasoning of our teacher the Ari, one should not say 'safek berachot lehakel.' And see what we wrote further ahead regarding the blessing 'she'asah li kol tzorki.'

clarification.explanation: The blessing 'Pokei'ach Ivrim' — thanksgiving for the opening of the eyes from sleep. There is a dispute whether a blind person recites it; the halachah is — he blesses (according to the opinion of the Ari that these blessings were instituted according to the custom of the world, and not only for one who is personally obligated in them).
takeaways: A blind person recites 'Pokei'ach Ivrim' even though he does not personally benefit, because the blessing was instituted according to the custom of the world.

paragraphs: If one recited 'Zokef Kefufim' before 'Matir Assurim,' he should not recite 'Matir Assurim,' because being bent over is more severe than being bound, and since he has recited 'Zokef,' it is included within the greater [category]. However, it is good to recite 'Matir Assurim' without [mentioning] the Name and Kingship, but rather he should meditate on the Name and Kingship in his heart, so that he not lack the number of lights alluded to by these blessings upon him; and furthermore, there are the Rashal and the Bach who ruled that one should bless — therefore, in order to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions, he should bless without the Name and Kingship and merely meditate on the Name and Kingship within the blessing. And even a person who is bound in any case due to illness, unable to move from his bed, likewise recites this blessing, for these blessings were instituted according to the custom of the world; see Minchat Aharon, Klal 5, letter 14.

clarification.explanation: If one recited 'Zokef Kefufim' before 'Matir Assurim' (out of order) — he should not recite 'Matir Assurim' again (since being bent is more severe than being bound, and it is already included). Nevertheless, it is good to recite 'Matir Assurim' without the Name and Kingship (and meditate upon them in his heart), in order to satisfy all opinions. Even a person confined to bed due to illness recites this blessing (according to the custom of the world).
takeaways: If one erred in the order of blessings (Zokef before Matir) — he completes 'Matir Assurim' without the Name and Kingship, meditating on them.

paragraphs: If at the time he said 'Baruch Atah Hashem' his intention was to bless 'Zokef Kefufim,' he should conclude with 'Zokef Kefufim,' even though he will then be unable to bless 'Matir Assurim' [separately] — so wrote Rabbi Chayei Adam, Klal 8, letter 5, see there. And in my holy book Makbetzi'el, I raised that one should not rely on this to lose the second blessing, and only, indeed, one must be careful ab initio not to say 'Baruch Atah Hashem' except with intention to conclude the correct blessing which he needs to bless, with intention at the mentioning of the Name.

clarification.explanation: If at the beginning of 'Baruch Atah Hashem' one intended 'Zokef Kefufim,' he should conclude accordingly (even though he will then be unable to bless 'Matir Assurim' separately) — but one should not rely on this and lose a blessing; ab initio one must be careful that the intention at the mentioning of the Name be for the conclusion of the correct blessing from the outset.
takeaways: One must have in mind in advance which blessing he is reciting before saying 'Baruch Atah Hashem,' so as not to lose a blessing.

paragraphs: After 'Malbish Arumim' one recites 'HaNotein LaYa'ef Koach' (Who gives strength to the weary), and these two blessings were instituted regarding the garments of the soul, for there is a person who loses the garment of his soul entirely, and the Holy One, blessed be He, in His kindness gives it a new garment, for it is naked; and there is one who does not sin so much as to lose the garment entirely, but only weakens it, and the Holy One, blessed be He, in His kindness gives him strength to strengthen it every day, as He returns his soul to him in the morning.

clarification.explanation: After 'Malbish Arumim' one blesses 'HaNotein LaYa'ef Koach' — these two blessings relate to 'the garments of the soul': one who loses the garment of his soul entirely receives, by God's kindness, a new garment; one who only weakens it receives renewed strength every morning.
takeaways: 'Malbish Arumim' and 'HaNotein LaYa'ef Koach' relate to the 'garment of the soul,' which is renewed/strengthened every morning.

paragraphs: The blessing 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki' was instituted regarding the putting on of shoes, for one who is barefoot cannot attend to his needs and the needs of his household, and since he has put on his shoes, it is as though all his needs have been met, for then he is ready to go wherever he wishes, as mentioned in Shalmei Tzibbur. And our teacher, may his memory be blessed, wrote in Sha'ar HaKavanot, page 2 column 4: 'All eighteen blessings that exist from "Al Netilat Yadayim" until the end of the blessing of the Torah, a person is obligated to arrange and recite them every day, even though he was not obligated in them, because they are all wondrous allusions to supernal lights, and one must not omit them even if the person did not sleep at night, or if he did not remove his turban or his garments or his scarf or his shoes, and the like — he must recite them all every day, even though he was not obligated in them, because they were instituted according to the custom of the world — except for the blessing "She'asah Li Kol Tzorki" on the Ninth of Av and on Yom Kippur, when the entire world goes barefoot; and also except for the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar," these two, which if he was not obligated in them, one should not bless over them' — until here his words. It is clearly proven from his words that a mourner should recite 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki,' since the entire world wears shoes, and only on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur, even though the sick and a woman in childbirth wear [shoes] as a minority exception, and the entire world cannot draw down the lights of this blessing because of these few who wear shoes; and so too in Shalmei Tzibbur it was proven from the words of our teacher, may his memory be blessed, that a mourner blesses, see there. However, the pious Rabbi, Mahar"a Sharabi, may his memory be blessed, in the book Divrei Shalom, page 64, explained the intentions of our teacher, may his memory be blessed, that he requires that this person derive at least some benefit from the thing over which he is blessing, and therefore he ruled and taught that a mourner should not bless, since he does not benefit; and in my book Makbetzi'el I brought his words and resolved the precise wording of our teacher's words properly, and I raised doubts about the words of the Rabbi of Divrei Shalom mentioned, and I argued against him that even according to his understanding, the mourner also benefits from this, since others wear shoes and attend to his needs, which would not be so if they were barefoot; and likewise the blind man blesses 'Pokei'ach Ivrim' because he benefits from the opening of others' eyes; and I concluded, as the essential ruling, that a mourner blesses, and so the people practice.

clarification.explanation: The blessing 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki' was instituted regarding putting on shoes — for one who is barefoot cannot attend to his needs, and since he put on his shoes it is as if all his needs were met (ready to go wherever he wishes) (Shalmei Tzibbur). The Ari (Sha'ar HaKavanot) wrote that all eighteen blessings from 'Al Netilat Yadayim' until the end of the blessing of the Torah must be arranged and recited every day, even though one was not obligated in them, for they are all wondrous allusions to supernal lights and must not be omitted — even if one did not sleep, did not remove his garments/shoes, etc. — for they were instituted according to the custom of the world; except for 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki' on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur (when everyone is barefoot), and except for 'Al Netilat Yadayim' and 'Asher Yatzar' (which, if one was not obligated in them, should not be blessed). It is proven that a mourner blesses 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki,' since the entire world wears shoes (and only on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur are the sick and women in childbirth, who wear shoes, a negligible minority, unable to sustain the blessing for everyone). However, Rabbi Sharabi ('Divrei Shalom') explained that the Ari requires that the one blessing actually benefit from the matter, and therefore ruled that a mourner does not bless, since he does not benefit; but the Ben Ish Chai ('Makbetzi'el') disagreed, holding that the mourner too benefits — since others wear shoes and attend to his needs (unlike if they were barefoot) — just as a blind person blesses 'Pokei'ach Ivrim' because he benefits from others' sight — and concluded that the essential ruling is that a mourner blesses, and so the people practice.
takeaways: 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki' was instituted regarding putting on shoes; one recites all the morning blessings every day even though not obligated (according to 'the custom of the world').
Exceptions: 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki' on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur, and 'Al Netilat Yadayim' and 'Asher Yatzar' (only if obligated).
A mourner recites 'She'asah Li Kol Tzorki' (since he benefits from others attending to his needs) — and so is the practical ruling.

paragraphs: Although the Acharonim raised that if one recited 'she'lo asani ishah' (who has not made me a woman), he should not recite the blessing over a gentile and a slave; and likewise, if he recited over a slave, he should not recite over a gentile — nevertheless he should recite [the omitted blessing] without [mentioning] the Name and Kingship, and meditate upon the Name and Kingship within the blessing. And women recite 'she'asani kirtzono' (who has made me according to His will) without the Name and Kingship, since there is a dispute about this, and [we follow the rule of] doubt regarding blessings, to be lenient; and it is good to meditate on the Name and Kingship within the blessing.

clarification.explanation: One who blessed 'she'lo asani ishah' should not bless 'she'lo asani eved' and 'she'lo asani goy'; and one who blessed 'she'lo asani eved' should not bless 'she'lo asani goy.' The exemption runs in one direction only: 'she'lo asani goy' does not exempt the other two. Nevertheless, one recites them without the Name and Kingship and meditates upon the Name and Kingship in his heart. Women bless 'she'asani kirtzono' without the Name and Kingship (there being a dispute, and doubt regarding blessings is resolved leniently).
takeaways: 'She'lo asani ishah' exempts [the need for] 'eved' and 'goy,' and 'she'lo asani eved' exempts 'goy' — but not the reverse, and 'she'lo asani goy' exempts nothing; women bless 'she'asani kirtzono' without the Name and Kingship.

paragraphs: The blessing 'HaMaavir' (who removes sleep) concludes with 'Baruch Gomel Chasadim Tovim' etc., and therefore one does not answer Amen after 'u'tenumah mei'af'apai' [and slumber from my eyelids], and one must say 'Vayehi Ratzon' with a vav [and]; he should also say 'HaMaavir' etc. in the singular, saying 'mei'einai' and 'me'af'apai,' and likewise 'targileini,' 'tadbikeini,' and the rest, in the wording of 'Vayehi Ratzon' etc., for this is the version of our Sages in the Talmud, and so it is in the siddur of our teacher HaRashash, may his memory be blessed; and see Divrei Shalom, page 65, what he wrote about this, see there.

clarification.explanation: The blessing 'HaMaavir Sheinah Mei'einai' concludes with 'Baruch Gomel Chasadim Tovim Le'amo Yisrael'; one does not answer Amen after 'u'tenumah mei'af'apai' (which is not the end of the blessing). One must say 'Vayehi Ratzon' (with a vav) in the singular ('mei'einai,' 'me'af'apai,' 'targileini,' 'tadbikeini') following the version of our Sages.
takeaways: The blessing 'HaMaavir Sheinah' is recited in the singular through the end of 'Vayehi Ratzon'; one does not answer Amen in the middle (only at the end).

paragraphs: Although one must say 've'ha'arev' with a vav, nevertheless these are two blessings, and one answers Amen after the first blessing, before 've'ha'arev.' And before the blessing of the Torah, one should not study either the Written Torah or the Oral Torah; to render a legal ruling without giving the reason is permitted, but if he states the reason, it is forbidden; and likewise to write words of Torah, or to hear them, is also forbidden without the blessing of the Torah — but mere contemplation (hirhur) is permitted; and some say that this permission for hirhur applies only if he contemplates in his heart alone, without looking into a book. And women also recite the blessing of the Torah. And if one slept during the day on his bed a fixed sleep (sheinat keva), there is a dispute whether it is considered an interruption requiring him to bless again or not; and since [we follow the rule of] doubt regarding blessings, to be lenient, he should bless without the Name and Kingship and meditate on the Name and Kingship in his heart. And one whom sleep overtook in the midst of the morning blessings — then, regarding any blessing about which he is in doubt whether he recited it or not, he should not bless out of doubt, even if he is in doubt about the blessing of the Torah; and in any case he should bless without the Name and Kingship and meditate on the Name and Kingship within the blessing. And if he forgot and did not recite the morning blessings before prayer, he should recite them after prayer, except for the blessing 'HaMachazir Neshamot' (who returns souls), for he is exempted by the blessing 'Mechayeh HaMeitim' [within the Amidah], and except for the blessing of the Torah, which is exempted by [the blessing] 'Ahavat Olam.'

clarification.explanation: Although one says 've'ha'arev' with a vav — it is nevertheless two blessings, and one answers Amen after the first, before 've'ha'arev.' And before the blessing of the Torah one may not study Written or Oral Torah; to rule on a matter of law without stating the reason is permitted, but to state the reason is forbidden; likewise to write words of Torah or to hear them is forbidden without the blessing of the Torah — but mere contemplation is permitted (and some say this permission applies only if he contemplates in his heart alone, without looking into a book). Women too recite the blessing of the Torah. And if one slept a fixed sleep during the day on his bed — there is a dispute whether this constitutes an interruption requiring him to bless again; and since doubt regarding blessings is resolved leniently, he should bless without the Name and Kingship and meditate on the Name and Kingship in his heart. And one whom sleep overtook in the midst of the morning blessings — any blessing about which he is in doubt whether he recited it, he should not bless out of doubt (and even regarding the blessing of the Torah — he should bless without the Name and Kingship and meditate upon them). And if he forgot and did not recite the morning blessings before prayer, he should recite them after prayer, except for 'HaMachazir Neshamot' (exempted by 'Mechayeh HaMeitim') and the blessing of the Torah (exempted by 'Ahavat Olam').
takeaways: 'Ve'ha'arev' is a second blessing — one answers Amen after the first; and before the blessing of the Torah one may not study (though contemplation is permitted), and women recite it.
One who slept a fixed sleep during the day — it is in doubt whether he must bless again; he should bless without the Name and Kingship and meditate upon them.
One who forgot the morning blessings — he recites them after prayer, except for 'HaMachazir Neshamot' (exempted by 'Mechayeh HaMeitim') and the blessing of the Torah (exempted by 'Ahavat Olam').

paragraphs: One who slept at night on his bed a fixed sleep and awoke before midnight should not recite the morning blessings — so it appears from the unqualified words of the Kabbalists, and so it appears from the words of the holy Zohar, Bereishit, page 10, column 2; see Mikdash Melech there. But the blessing of the Torah he may recite before midnight, since he has already slept a fixed sleep, as appears from the holy Zohar there; see the Acharonim. However, if he awakens close to midnight, it is proper for him to wait until after midnight, in order to recite the morning blessings together with the blessing of the Torah in the order of the fixed daily arrangement, so that they be a single connected unit; and if he wishes, in this brief interim period, he may recite verses of song and praise. And I asked our beloved friend, the Gaon, the pious Rabbi, our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may the Merciful One preserve and redeem him, regarding the custom of the pious ones (the Chasidim) in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and established speedily in our days, and he answered as follows: 'Among both the plain-sense scholars and the Kabbalists, all agree that if one slept a fixed sleep he is obligated to bless and is able to bless, as appears from the language of the holy Zohar, Part 1, page 10, column 2; see Mikdash Melech. However, there are two intentions in the blessing of the Torah: one particular, which is mentioned in Nahar Shalem, page 92 column 1, and this applies even before midnight; and one general, included within the eighteen blessings, mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot, Jerusalem printing, page 1, column 3; and see Nahar Shalom, page 39 column 2 and page 87 column 2, for their explanation. And certainly one who blesses before midnight does not achieve this repair (tikkun), since if the supernal ones have not yet been repaired, how can those below be repaired? Nevertheless, the custom in Beit El, may it be built and established speedily, is that when it is close to midnight, some recite the blessing of the Torah and study, and at midnight they recite the other blessings; and there are pious ones who nevertheless wait until midnight for the sake of the repair of the order of the eighteen blessings' — until here his language, may the Merciful One preserve and redeem him.

clarification.explanation: One who slept a fixed sleep at night and awoke before midnight should not recite the morning blessings (as follows from the unqualified words of the Kabbalists and from the Zohar), but he may recite the blessing of the Torah already, since the sleep itself is considered an interruption justifying the blessing. One who awakens close to midnight — it is proper that he wait until after midnight and recite all the blessings (morning and Torah) together, in the fixed daily order, so that they be joined as one; and in the brief interim while he waits, it is good to recite verses of song and praise. And the inner reason for the distinction regarding the blessing of the Torah: Rabbi Eliyahu Mani explains that there are two different intentions within the blessing of the Torah — one 'particular' (relating to the person himself), which applies and is effective even before midnight; and the second 'general,' relating to the overall repair of the order of the eighteen blessings (as alluded to in the Kabbalistic intentions), which is attained only after midnight — because 'the supernal ones have not yet been repaired' at that hour (the repair above is not yet complete), and consequently those below (the blessing here below) cannot complete it beforehand either. For this reason, in Beit El (the fellowship of Kabbalists in Jerusalem) the custom was: one who awakens close to midnight recites the blessing of the Torah and studies Torah already before midnight (since thereby he achieves the particular intention), and waits specifically until midnight for the other blessings; and there are some of the pious who are stringent and wait until midnight even for the blessing of the Torah itself, in order to merit also the complete general repair.
takeaways: One who slept a fixed sleep and awoke before midnight: he should not recite the morning blessings, but he may recite the blessing of the Torah.
Close to midnight — it is preferable to wait and recite all the blessings together after midnight, in the fixed order.

The Kabbalistic reason: the blessing of the Torah has a particular intention (effective even before midnight) and a general intention relating to the overall repair of the eighteen blessings (attained only after midnight).

In Beit El the custom was to recite the blessing of the Torah before midnight and study, and to wait until midnight for the other blessings; and some wait until midnight even for the blessing of the Torah.

paragraphs: A person is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day, and on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when they are lacking due to [the shortened] blessings of the Amidah, he should then make them up with kinds of fruit and pleasant fragrance. And behold, it is explained in the words of our teacher, may his memory be blessed, in Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh, page 4 column 1, and this is his language: 'Know that the twenty-two letters of the alphabet are dependent upon the hundred blessings which a person blesses every day, and when a person does not recite at all some blessing among them, that letter upon which that blessing depends is lacking from him; and if he recited the letter but erred in it, then that letter will be present, but it will itself be deficient; and if he recited it correctly but did not have intention in it, then that letter will be present but dark and unilluminated' — until here his language. And from this you may understand how much a person must exert himself regarding the hundred blessings.

clarification.explanation: A person is obligated to recite one hundred blessings every day (on Shabbat/Yom Tov, what is lacking from the Amidah is made up with fruits and pleasant fragrance). According to the secret, the twenty-two letters of the alphabet are dependent upon the hundred daily blessings: a blessing not recited at all — its corresponding letter is lacking; a blessing recited in error — the letter is present but flawed; a blessing recited correctly but without intention — the letter is present but dark and unilluminated.
takeaways: Each of the hundred daily blessings is connected to a letter of the alphabet; precision and intention in the blessing affect the state of that letter (whole/flawed/dark).

paragraphs: I found it written that it is good for a person to accustom himself to say every day these three verses written in 1 Chronicles chapter 29: 'And David blessed the Lord before all the assembly, and David said, Blessed are You, O Lord,' etc., 'Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power,' etc., 'and the riches and the honor come from You,' etc. — as our Sages instituted them in the Zemirot said every day — and a person should say them by themselves each day ten or seven times, and each time say after them the verse 'Baruch Atah Hashem, lamdeini chukecha' (Blessed are You, O Lord, teach me Your statutes); and besides the mystical benefit there is in reciting them, it will also help him to complete the number of one hundred blessings in a time of pressing need — until here what I found; and it seems to me that this is a fine and correct custom; and see Pitchei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah, siman 328, small letter 1, what he wrote in the name of Rabbi Peri Tevuah, what he received from his teachers, see there. I also found it written in Keter Malchut, in manuscript, a fine custom, that a person say every day the verse 'Baruch Hashem le'olam, amen ve'amen' (Psalms 89:53) forty-five times, and when saying 'amen ve'amen' he should have intention with the combined Name of Havayah-Adonai; and this verse will benefit him in place of ninety 'amens' which a person is obligated to say every day, at a time when he is prevented by circumstance and unable to answer [them], such as one who sits alone at home and does not go to the synagogue due to circumstances beyond his control — until here. And it seems to me that this is a fine custom, and so I have practiced, to say this verse the aforementioned number of times every day after the passage of the Priestly Blessing which we say after the morning blessings every day; and I did so in order that its recitation not be forgotten by me, since I set for it a fixed time; and after this verse I say the verse 'Or zarua latzaddik' (Psalms 97:11) seventeen times, as the Gaon Rabbi Chaim Palaggi, may his memory be blessed, wrote, that it is proper to say it seventeen times every day.

clarification.explanation: The Ben Ish Chai found it written that it is fitting to accustom oneself to say every day these three verses (1 Chronicles 29): 'And David blessed the Lord before all the assembly... Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power... and the riches and the honor come from You...' — as our Sages instituted them within the Zemirot — and to say them by themselves ten or seven times, and each time afterward 'Baruch Atah Hashem, lamdeini chukecha'; and besides the mystical benefit, this also helps to complete the hundred blessings in a time of pressing need. He also found it written in Keter Malchut a fine custom, to say every day the verse 'Baruch Hashem le'olam, amen ve'amen' forty-five times, having intention at 'amen ve'amen' with the combined Name Havayah-Adonai; and this verse benefits in place of the ninety 'amens' a person is obligated to say every day, when he is prevented by circumstance and unable to answer (such as one sitting alone at home who does not go to the synagogue due to circumstances beyond his control). And the Ben Ish Chai likewise practiced saying it forty-five times every day after the Priestly Blessing recited after the morning blessings (at a fixed time, so as not to forget), and afterward says 'Or zarua latzaddik' seventeen times (following the view of Rabbi Chaim Palaggi).
takeaways: A fine custom: to say every day the three verses 'Vayevarech David... Lecha Hashem hagedulah...' (7 or 10 times, followed each time by 'lamdeini chukecha') — also to help complete the hundred blessings in a time of pressing need.

'Baruch Hashem le'olam, amen ve'amen' 45 times (with intention on the Name Havayah-Adonai) — benefits in place of the 90 'amens' for one prevented by circumstance; followed by 'Or zarua latzaddik' seventeen times.
